articles.title: Ultrasound quantification of liver fat in MASLD.
articles.abstract: Metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD) is highly prevalent and frequently first recognized at ultrasound, but conventional B-mode assessment is limited by subjectivity and reduced sensitivity for mild steatosis. Quantitative ultrasound (QUS) techniques address these limitations by converting acoustic signal properties into numerical biomarkers of hepatic fat, including attenuation coefficient, backscatter coefficient, speed of sound, and composite measures. This review summarizes the technical principles, current evidence, clinical implementation, and limitations of ultrasound-based liver fat quantification techniques in MASLD. Their major advantages are accessibility, integration into routine ultrasound examinations, and potential use alongside elastography for multiparametric assessment. However, thresholds vary across vendors, software implementations, acquisition protocols, reference standards, and patient populations, limiting interchangeability and universal cutoffs. In clinical practice, ultrasound fat quantification should not be interpreted in isolation but integrated with fibrosis risk stratification and metabolic risk assessment. Further multicenter studies are needed to standardize acquisition and reporting, define clinically meaningful longitudinal changes, and link ultrasound-derived fat reduction with patient outcomes. QUS is therefore best regarded as an evolving, practical framework for objective steatosis assessment that complements, rather than replaces, comprehensive MASLD risk stratification. KEY POINTS: Question Conventional B-mode ultrasound is subjective and insensitive to mild hepatic steatosis, creating an unmet need for objective, reproducible liver fat quantification in MASLD. Findings Attenuation-based and composite quantitative ultrasound methods provide objective liver fat assessment, but vendor-dependent thresholds currently limit interchangeability and universal clinical application. Clinical relevance Quantitative ultrasound enables accessible, objective liver fat assessment during routine imaging, improving detection and grading of hepatic steatosis and supporting risk-based MASLD care; however, vendor-specific thresholds and acquisition variability require technique-specific interpretation.

articles.title: Comprehensive reporting of acute aortic syndromes: a practical approach for radiologists.
articles.abstract: Acute aortic syndromes (AAS) are a group of aortic pathologies with high morbidity and mortality. In the emergency setting, an accurate diagnosis is usually achieved by aortic computed tomography angiography (CTA). Recently, reporting and management guidelines have evolved due to modifications in surgical techniques and the expansion in utilization of endovascular techniques. This being said, radiologists require a more in-depth knowledge of key points to report to surgeons, their clinical implications, and some insights into available imaging-guided treatment options. Given the urgent nature of AAS, the need for rapid, detailed, and standardized reporting is crucial. In this review, we aim to introduce a step-by-step approach to accurate reporting of AAS, discussing recent guidelines and the role of imaging in the preprocedural evaluation of each disease entity (namely, intramural hematoma, penetrating aortic ulcer, and aortic dissection). Additionally, we will highlight the role of key imaging findings in the management of each disease entity. KEY POINTS: Question Acute aortic syndromes require rapid, sufficiently detailed, and accurate diagnosis to allow for timely patient management. Findings In this article, we propose a step-by-step approach using a structured reporting checklist. Clinical relevance Using a stepwise approach will allow timely reporting, give important details, and help guide further patient care.

articles.title: In Vivo Ankle Tendon Quantification Using Ultrashort Echo Time Magnetization Transfer Imaging.
articles.abstract: OBJECTIVES: To quantitatively assess in vivo ankle tendons using less magic angle-sensitive 3-dimensional ultrashort echo time magnetization transfer (UTE MT) imaging and to compare its intersubject variability with UTE T2* mapping in healthy volunteers. MATERIALS AND METHODS: Thirty healthy volunteer ankles were examined on a 3T MRI system using a standardized clinical protocol with additional 3D UTE MT and 3D multi-echo UTE T2* sequences (acquisition times: 4:16 and 9:52 minutes, respectively). Nine major ankle tendons were semi-automatically segmented to extract quantitative UTE MTR and UTE T2* values for each tendon. Variability for each sequence was assessed using the coefficient of variation (CV), and differences in CV were evaluated primarily with a paired bootstrap of the CV ratio and secondarily with a modified signed log-likelihood ratio (MSLR) test, both with Holm correction. Within-tendon angular dependence was assessed using local tendon fiber angles relative to B0. RESULTS: Absolute quantitative values differed between tendons, with the Achilles tendon demonstrating the lowest T2* values (2.15±0.43 ms) and highest MTR values (0.44±0.08), whereas smaller positional tendons showed higher T2* and lower MTR values. UTE MTR demonstrated lower overall variability compared with UTE T2* values across the 9 assessed tendons (overall CV UTE MTR: 18.0%±4.2% vs. UTE T2*: 33.7%±8.9%, mean±SD, n=9). In the paired bootstrap analysis with Holm correction, UTE MTR showed significantly lower variability than UTE T2* in 6 of 9 tendons, with the largest differences in the extensor digitorum longus, peroneus brevis, and flexor hallucis longus tendons (T2*/MTR CV ratio, 2.74, 2.60, and 2.48; all Holm-adjusted P≤0.015); MSLR results were consistent. Between 0 degree and the magic angle, UTE T2* increased by 79% (95% CI: 64%-95%), whereas UTE MTR decreased by 9% (95% CI: 7%-11%). UTE MTR consistently demonstrated reduced dispersion and narrower value distributions compared with UTE T2*. CONCLUSIONS: In vivo ankle tendon quantification using UTE MT is feasible within clinically acceptable acquisition times and shows significantly lower intersubject variability than UTE T2* mapping in most tendons, with reduced susceptibility to the magic angle effect. UTE MT represents a promising approach for quantitative assessment of tendon structure in vivo.

articles.title: Photon-Counting CT for Postoperative Imaging of Cochlear Implants: Comparison to Flat-Detector CT.
articles.abstract: OBJECTIVES: After FDA approval in 2021, photon-counting detector computed tomography (PCCT) has demonstrated its feasibility for high-resolution imaging while lowering the radiation dose at the same time. High-resolution visualization of cochlear implant (CI) integrity and positioning is crucial for postoperative management. The aim of this study was to evaluate the performance of PCCT for postoperative imaging after CI implantation in comparison to high-resolution flat-detector CT (FDCT), the current clinical gold standard. MATERIALS AND METHODS: Postoperative PCCT scans after cochlear implantation were retrospectively analyzed from August 2024 to April 2026. Scans were included for analysis if FDCT acquisition had been before PCCT on the same patient in the course of sequential bilateral cochlear implantation. Image quality was assessed in consensus by 2 experienced readers using a scoring system analyzing structural delineation of the inner and middle ear, CI integrity, metal and motion artifacts as well as calculating an overall score. Radiation dose was retrieved from the picture archiving and communication system. RESULTS: Twenty-eight postoperative PCCT scans of patients after CI implantation with a mean time delay of 4.5±5.1 years between FDCT and PCCT scans were evaluated. Image quality of PCCT was noninferior to FDCT for all single imaging features (P<0.001, eg, distinction of single CI electrodes: median [interquartile range] PCCT 3 [3 to 3]; FDCT 3 [3 to 3]; P<0.001) with the exception of the homogeneity of bony structures and the mastoid cell septation (P=0.999). PCCT was superior to FDCT in reducing metal and motion artifacts and increasing the delineation of the stapes (P=0.009 to <0.001; eg, metal artifacts PCCT 3 [2.75 to 3]; FDCT 2 [1 to 2]; P<0.001). Effective radiation dose of PCCT was 0.05±0.01 mSv and 8.8±5.4-times lower than for FDCT with 0.44±0.29 mSv (P<0.001) applying our institutional protocols. CONCLUSIONS: Regarding image quality in postoperative assessment of CI, PCCT is noninferior to or in single features better than FDCT at a significantly lower radiation dose and shorter scan time.

articles.title: Delayed hepatobiliary phase imaging improves bile leak detection on gadoxetate-enhanced MRI.
articles.abstract: OBJECTIVES: To compare conventional and delayed (≥ 30 min) hepatobiliary-phase (HBP) gadoxetate-enhanced MRI for the detection of bile leaks. MATERIALS AND METHODS: This retrospective single-center study included all consecutive gadoxetate-enhanced MRI examinations comprising delayed HBP acquisitions performed for suspected biliary leak over 2 years at a tertiary hepatobiliary referral center. Two abdominal radiologists blinded to clinical records independently assessed leak presence at each timepoint. A composite reference standard incorporating endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography, surgical exploration, percutaneous drainage findings, and multidisciplinary assessment was utilized to assign ground-truth leak status. Sensitivity, specificity, positive and negative predictive values (PPV, NPV), accuracy, and inter-reader agreement were calculated. RESULTS: Thirty-five patients (22 men; median age, 56 years; interquartile range (IQR), 48-65) undergoing 36 examinations were included. The most common indications were liver transplantation (n = 13/35, 37%) and cholecystectomy (n = 11/35, 31%). Conventional and delayed HBP were acquired at a median of 21 and 65 min after injection, respectively. Twenty-two of 36 examinations (61%) were ground-truth positive. Inter-reader agreement was perfect for conventional HBP (κ = 1.00) and excellent for delayed HBP (κ = 0.94; 95% CI 0.84-1.00). Conventional HBP demonstrated 27% sensitivity (95% CI 11-50%), 100% specificity (95% CI 77-100%), and 56% accuracy (95% CI 38-72%). Delayed HBP demonstrated 82% sensitivity (95% CI 60-95%), 100% specificity (95% CI 77-100%), and 89% accuracy (95% CI 74-97%). NPV increased from 47% to 78%. Delayed HBP yielded higher sensitivity and overall accuracy than conventional HBP (p < 0.001, exact McNemar tests). CONCLUSION: Delayed HBP improved bile leak detection without loss of specificity. KEY POINTS: Question Does extending gadoxetate hepatobiliary-phase MRI acquisitions beyond the conventional 20-min window improve the detection of active bile leaks? Findings Delayed hepatobiliary-phase imaging raised sensitivity for bile leak detection from 27% to 82% without loss of specificity, highlighting acquisition timing as a key diagnostic determinant. Clinical relevance Delayed gadoxetate hepatobiliary-phase imaging is an effective adjunct for detecting active bile leaks and should be considered when findings at conventional timing are negative or equivocal, with direct implications for clinical management.

articles.title: Three-dimensional automated muscle and adipose analysis to predict hepatic encephalopathy after transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunt.
articles.abstract: OBJECTIVES: Overt hepatic encephalopathy (HE) limits the use of transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunt (TIPS) in portal hypertension. We aimed to determine whether automated three-dimensional (3D) body composition analysis could improve pre-TIPS prediction of overt HE compared with conventional two-dimensional (2D) manual assessment. MATERIALS AND METHODS: This multicenter study included 593 eligible patients from seven institutions (training cohort: n = 308; external validation 1 cohort: n = 151; and external validation 2 cohort: n = 134). After evaluating L3-based 2D measurements, we developed a fully automated 3D muscle and adipose assessment incorporating morphologic and radiomic features. We combined the 3D assessment with selected clinical variables to predict post-TIPS overt HE risk, and benchmarked the final model against published clinical scores. Model performance was evaluated via ROC analysis, DeLong tests, calibration, decision curve analysis, and subgroup analyses. RESULTS: Traditional 2D measurements showed poor reproducibility, with significant variation in 96.2% (25/26) of features. The 3D Model significantly outperformed the 2D Model. The Integrated Model yielded AUCs of 0.78, 0.73, and 0.77 in the training and two external validation cohorts, exceeding those of Child-Pugh, MELD, ALBI, AMMON-OHE, and Lambda (AUCs 0.47-0.64; all p < 0.05). No significant subgroup differences were observed. High-risk patients had 2- to 4-fold higher overt HE incidence. The model reclassified 40.2% of patients with low pre-TIPS ammonia as high risk and 60.2% of those with high ammonia as low risk. CONCLUSION: Automated 3D muscle and adipose analysis enables objective preprocedural prediction of overt HE after TIPS, which may facilitate clinical decision-making and optimize patient selection. KEY POINTS: Question Can automated three-dimensional muscle and adipose analysis improve reproducible preprocedural prediction of overt hepatic encephalopathy after transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunt beyond conventional two-dimensional assessment? Findings In 593 patients from seven hospitals, an Integrated Model combining automated three-dimensional body composition and clinical variables outperformed five published clinical comparator scores. Clinical relevance This fully automated three-dimensional body composition (muscle and adipose) analysis enables objective preprocedural risk stratification for overt hepatic encephalopathy after transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunt, supporting more consistent patient selection.

articles.title: A nomogram integrating clinical and radiological data to predict long-term infliximab efficacy in Crohn's disease.
articles.abstract: OBJECTIVES: Infliximab (IFX) is a monoclonal antibody to treat Crohn's disease (CD), but loss of response is common. We aimed to develop an effective nomogram to predict long-term outcomes of IFX. MATERIALS AND METHODS: A retrospective observational study was conducted on CD patients receiving regular IFX. The endpoint was defined as loss of response within 78 weeks, further classified as uncomplicated or complicated. Baseline characteristics, pre- and postinduction clinical indicators, and computed tomography enterography imaging features were collected. Candidate predictors were selected using the least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (LASSO) regression and multivariable logistic regression to construct a clinical-radiological nomogram, validated using receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analysis, decision curve analysis, and calibration plots. Kaplan-Meier analysis evaluated the clinical implications of predictor cut-off values. RESULTS: The study enrolled 165 patients, with 112 in the training cohort and 53 in the validation cohort. LASSO-logistic regression revealed erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) at week 14 and maximum small bowel wall thickness (SBWT-max) at baseline as independent predictors of long-term non-response. The nomogram achieved an area under the curve (AUC) of 0.834 (training) and 0.913 (validation) for loss of response, and 0.746 and 0.876 for uncomplicated and complicated loss of response, respectively. Validation of the nomogram confirmed its discriminative, calibrating, and clinical utility. Additionally, ESR at week 14 > 10.5 mm/h or baseline SBWT-max > 7.5 mm showed reduced response duration. CONCLUSIONS: The feasible nomogram combining ESR postinduction and SBWT-max at baseline effectively predicts long-term efficacy of IFX, which guides the therapy for CD patients. KEY POINTS: QuestionLoss of response to infliximab is common in Crohn's disease, yet a reliable tool to predict long-term efficacy and guide timely therapeutic decisions remains rare. FindingsA nomogram based on LASSO-logistic regression integrating postinduction ESR and baseline maximum small bowel wall thickness accurately predicted long-term loss of response, including complicated failure. Clinical relevanceThis validated nomogram enables early, risk-stratified identification of patients likely to develop uncomplicated versus complicated loss of response, guiding proactive therapy switch and personalized management in Crohn's disease.

articles.title: Tuda: Tucker-parameterized unified dual-stream asymmetric architecture for label-free 3D subcellular structure prediction.
articles.abstract: Label-free prediction of three-dimensional subcellular fluorescence from transmitted-light microscopy enables scalable and less invasive live-cell analysis. However, building a unified subcellular structure prediction (SSP) model remains difficult: each training volume is only partially labeled, target organelles exhibit highly heterogeneous morphologies, and many structures require long-range topological coherence beyond local appearance. We propose TUDA, a unified dual-stream framework in which all components are conditioned on a shared learnable task embedding, enabling organelle-specific specialization throughout the network. The local stream uses a Tucker decomposition-based hypernetwork to synthesize organelle-specific convolutional kernels from the task embedding, achieving compact yet diverse feature extraction within a single shared model. Complementing this, the global stream introduces Flash-TAS (Flash Transformer with Topology-Aware Shift), a Transformer branch that captures long-range structural dependencies while preserving voxel-level spatial correspondence. A Fusion Bridge adaptively integrates both streams for voxel-wise fluorescence regression. On a public benchmark covering 12 subcellular structures, TUDA achieves state-of-the-art SSP performance, improving relative R2 over RepMode by 3.9% while using 75% fewer parameters, with notable gains on topologically complex targets such as actin filaments and tight junctions.

articles.title: MedReShaper: mesh-based AI for 3D anatomical shape completion in orbital fracture reconstruction with controlled technical validation.
articles.abstract: Accurate three-dimensional (3D) reconstruction of missing orbital anatomy is important for surgical planning and patient-specific implant (PSI) design. Existing approaches often rely on contralateral mirroring or statistical shape priors, which may be limited in bilateral or anatomically asymmetric cases. We introduce MedReShaper, a mesh-based AI method for direct unilateral orbital reconstruction from incomplete 3D surfaces using only preserved ipsilateral anatomical information. MedReShaper integrates anatomy-guided multi-view projections, ASC-Net, and multi-angle candidate refinement to reconstruct missing orbital geometry directly from incomplete meshes. The model was developed using 2,400 health unilateral orbital meshes from UZ Leuven and evaluated in three stages: controlled technical validation on 120 independent cases with intact orbital anatomy with virtual defects, multicenter external technical validation on 1,187 external cases with intact orbital anatomy from 12 external cohorts from multiple institutions and data sources using the same controlled-defect strategy, and retrospective clinical evaluation on 45 patients with genuine traumatic orbital fractures using expert-derived reference surfaces and independent surgeon assessment. In Stage I, mean point-cloud and surface errors were 0.46 ± 0.32 mm and 0.57 ± 0.38 mm, respectively. Broadly consistent performance was maintained across the Stage II external cohort, with mean center-level errors of 0.49 mm and 0.60 mm. In Stage III, MedReShaper achieved a full-surface error of 0.61 ± 0.43 mm and a mean reconstruction time of 54.1 ± 15.7 s per case, demonstrating competitive geometric accuracy with favorable clinical usability and reconstruction efficiency. These results demonstrate robust technical performance across independent and multicenter datasets and provide initial clinical evidence supporting further evaluation of MedReShaper for orbital fracture reconstruction and surgical planning.

articles.title: LifespanFix: Semi-supervised cortical correction across the human lifespan.
articles.abstract: Accurate characterization of the cerebral cortex in brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is essential for reliable morphometric analyses across the human lifespan. However, the cortex's thin and highly convoluted architecture, together with imaging artifacts, frequently introduces topological and anatomical defects in segmentation that can bias downstream analyses. Here we present LifespanFix, a lifespan-robust cortical correction model that directly fixes topological and anatomical defects in segmentation. Specifically, we develop a semi-supervised framework in which a generation network produces template-constrained pseudo-labels that serve as structurally plausible targets for training a correction network (LifespanFix). During inference, only the trained LifespanFix model is deployed, enabling efficient end-to-end correction of cortical defects without requiring the generation network or the time-intensive registration used during training. Our framework was trained on 3,189 subjects spanning the human lifespan - from infancy to older adulthood - across nine public datasets. For evaluation, we assembled an independent lifespan testing cohort comprising 1,058 subjects from five datasets, including label maps generated by different segmentation methods. LifespanFix consistently outperforms state-of-the-art correction approaches, producing more accurate and anatomically plausible cortical segmentations across diverse ages, scanners, and imaging protocols, thereby enabling more reliable large-scale lifespan neuroimaging analyses.

articles.title: Endovascular treatment for cervical internal carotid artery occlusion due to dissection: a multicenter analysis.
articles.abstract: OBJECTIVE: Evidence on endovascular treatment (EVT) for isolated cervical internal carotid artery occlusion (c-ICA-O) due to dissection is limited. We evaluated the impact of EVT for dissection-related isolated (non-tandem) c-ICA-O. MATERIAL AND METHODS: This secondary analysis of the multicenter EVT for Isolated cervical Internal Carotid Artery occlusion (ETIICA) retrospective study included patients with dissections. Patients treated with EVT were compared with those treated with best medical treatment alone. The primary endpoint was 90-day modified Rankin Scale (mRS) shift analysis. Secondary outcomes included mRS 0-2 or return to baseline, early neurological deterioration (END), symptomatic intracerebral hemorrhage (sICH), carotid patency at the end of EVT, and intracranial embolization. Analyses used regressions with inverse probability of treatment weighting. RESULTS: Of 998 patients, 108 (10.8%) had dissection [mean age 53.7 (SD 11.2) years, 26.9% female]. EVT was performed in 60 (55.5%) patients. EVT patients had higher admission NIHSS (median 13 [4-18] vs 2 [0-9]). There was no difference in mRS shift (acOR 0.80, 95% CI: 0.29-2.20). Functional independence was observed in 64.9% of EVT patients vs 81.3% of BMT patients (aOR 1.69, 95% CI: 0.52-5.51; BMT as reference). END was numerically more frequent in the EVT group (28.8% vs 8.3%; aOR 2.38, 95% CI: 0.62-9.18). sICH occurred in 2 EVT patients. Carotid patency was achieved in 45/60 (75%) patients undergoing EVT, and 18/59 (30%) patients had intracranial embolization. CONCLUSION: In this exploratory analysis, EVT was not associated with improved 3-month functional outcomes, despite achieving carotid patency in three out of four patients. KEY POINTS: Question What are the technical and clinical outcomes of EVT compared with best medical treatment in patients with isolated cervical internal carotid artery occlusive dissection? Findings EVT effectively recanalized acutely occluded dissected extracranial internal carotid arteries, but intracranial emboli and re-occlusion were frequent, with no adjusted 90-day clinical benefit. Clinical relevance Precaution and technical refinement of EVT for isolated cervical carotid artery dissection appear necessary. Larger studies focusing on severely affected patients are warranted. Until such evidence is available, treatment decisions should be individualized on a case-by-case basis.

articles.title: Clinical applications of photon-counting CT in abdominal oncologic imaging: a primer for developing a clinical practice.
articles.abstract: Photon-counting CT (PCCT) is an emerging imaging modality that offers improved spatial resolution, soft tissue contrast, material decomposition, and dose efficiency over conventional CT with energy-integrating detectors (EID-CT). For patients with abdominal malignancies, who routinely undergo cross-sectional imaging for diagnosis, staging, response assessment, and surveillance, PCCT has the potential to enhance the detection and characterization of contrast-enhanced tumors and improve treatment response assessment. The objectives of this review are to provide a comprehensive overview of the technical principles of PCCT, optimization strategies, advantages in abdominal oncologic imaging, and current clinical applications geared towards clinical radiologists. We also address implementation challenges and discuss future directions for integrating PCCT into routine oncologic care. As PCCT utilization increases, its impact on abdominal cancer diagnosis and management is expected to grow, offering new opportunities for precision medicine and personalized imaging strategies.

articles.title: From features to digital biomarkers: EEG-fNIRS classification pipelines for brain monitoring.
articles.abstract: Electroencephalography (EEG) and functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) are widely used for noninvasive brain monitoring in clinical and cognitive applications, where machine learning-based classification has become increasingly prevalent. Alongside algorithmic advances, a growing body of literature reports signal-derived metrics as digital biomarkers; however, their interpretation, validity, and comparability remain strongly dependent on target definition, processing pipelines, and evaluation practices. This review provides a structured overview of EEG- and fNIRS-based classification studies, with a particular focus on signal processing workflows and biomarker extraction. The reviewed literature is organized around key stages of the analytical pipeline, including target formulation, data preprocessing, feature extraction, and validation. Common feature families-spanning spectral, temporal, connectivity-based, network-level, and hemodynamic representations-are summarized and discussed in relation to their typical applications and limitations. The main contribution is an evidence-based distinction between signal features and credible candidate biomarkers. Reliability, analytical robustness, external generalization, and interpretability are considered within the intended context of use. Clinical utility is assessed separately from predictive performance. Across 117 primary studies, most measures remained candidate biomarkers; only four studies were assigned to independent clinical validation, with qualifications, and none evaluated clinical utility.

articles.title: Image-guided ablation treatment of Desmoid tumors: an approach for management and integration into the national comprehensive cancer network ® guidelines.
articles.abstract: Desmoid tumors are proliferative mesenchymal tumors arising from musculoaponeurotic structures. Although lacking the ability to metastasize, these neoplasms have a propensity to locally invade and recur, resulting in significant morbidity and reduced quality of life. This variable natural history and unpredictable biologic behavior can complicate clinical management. Active surveillance may be appropriate as initial management, with systemic, surgical and other local treatment options considered depending on the extent of disease progression, in accordance with the current National Comprehensive Cancer Network guidelines. Notably, image-guided percutaneous cryoablation has emerged as an effective treatment option for rapid local control and sustained lesion regression. The efficacy of cryoablation in the management of these tumors is now supported by an increasing body of literature. This article will review the pathophysiology and natural history of desmoid tumors, together with treatment indications and national cancer guidelines. Image-guided ablation techniques will be described as well as how these options can fit into clinical paradigms and management pathways.

articles.title: Liver T1, T2, T2*, and PDFF Mapping at 0.55 T Using Rosette MRF With Optimized Sequence Design and Deep Image Reconstruction.
articles.abstract: PURPOSE: Quantitative imaging on mid-field (0.55 T) MRI systems can suffer from poor precision due to low SNR. This work presents an MRF pulse sequence optimized with Cramer-Rao lower bound (CRLB) and combined with a multi-echo deep image prior (DIP) reconstruction for co-registered T1/T2/T2*/PDFF mapping in the liver at 0.55 T within a single breath-hold. METHODS: A 20 s 2D multi-echo rosette MRF breath-hold acquisition was implemented on a 0.55 T wide-bore system. The sequence design was optimized via pseudorandom search using a CRLB-based objective for T1/T2 encoding and compared with reference designs. Data were reconstructed using (i) an iterative low-rank (LR) reconstruction and (ii) a multi-echo DIP jointly modeling TR- and echo-domain dynamics including B0 effects. Water/fat separation preceded dictionary matching for T1/T2; curve fitting was used to calculate T2* and PDFF was derived from M0 with noise-bias correction. The method was evaluated in numerical simulations, NIST and fat-fraction phantom scans, and in vivo acquisitions in 10 healthy subjects. A linear mixed-effects model was used to evaluate the effects of sequence design and reconstruction method on mapping accuracy and precision. RESULTS: Optimized sequences achieved lower CRLB cost than reference designs and, in simulations, CRLB cost was correlated with T1/T2 ROI variability (R2 = 0.76 LR; R2 = 0.83 DIP). Phantom experiments showed agreement with reference values. In vivo, both sequence optimization and DIP reconstruction significantly reduced the standard deviation of all four parameters in liver ROIs. CONCLUSION: CRLB-guided acquisition and multi-echo DIP reconstruction enable accurate and precise liver MRF T1/T2/T2*/PDFF mapping at 0.55 T in a single breath-hold.

articles.title: Improving Submillimeter BOLD fMRI Sensitivity With Localized Receive-Coil Design at 7 T.
articles.abstract: PURPOSE: To evaluate whether a dense, small-element receive array optimized for visual cortex imaging improves temporal SNR and BOLD sensitivity relative to a whole-head coil at 7 T, and whether this depends on spatial resolution. Two custom-built 7 T coils (32 receive, 8 transmit channels), one whole-head and one visual-cortex-optimized, were compared at 0.8- and 2.0-mm resolution. METHODS: Image SNR, temporal SNR, and BOLD sensitivity (suprathreshold spatial extent) were compared between coils at each resolution, acquired as a partial-slab protocol over the occipital lobe. RESULTS: The visual cortex coil yielded 2.5- and 2.8-fold higher image SNR at 0.8- and 2.0-mm resolution, respectively. At 0.8-mm, this only translated into a 1.3-fold increase in temporal SNR, but produced a 4.8-fold greater spatial extent of suprathreshold activation. Although contrast-to-noise-ratio (CNR) was only 2.4-fold higher for the visual cortex coil, decomposing CNR across the suprathreshold t-value distribution showed a 5.5-fold greater weighted CNR contribution, consistent with the larger spatial extent. At 2.0-mm resolution, temporal SNR was 1.4-fold higher with the visual cortex coil, but CNR and activation extent were similar between coils. CONCLUSION: The visual cortex coil's sensitivity advantage was higher at sub-millimeter resolution, where higher image SNR translated into higher temporal SNR and a 4.8-fold greater BOLD detection sensitivity, consistent with a 5.5-fold greater weighted CNR contribution across the suprathreshold t-value distribution. At 2.0-mm resolution, the SNR advantage did not translate into a detection benefit. The visual coil offers a practical advantage for ultra-high-field fMRI targeting fine-scale functional organization in the human visual cortex.

articles.title: Combining Cartesian and Non-Cartesian Acceleration Techniques With SPARKLING for 1 mm Isotropic Whole-Brain MPRAGE in a Minute.
articles.abstract: PURPOSE: T 1   -weighted MPRAGE remains a cornerstone of clinical anatomical imaging, yet its long acquisition times constrain routine use. Established acceleration techniques, namely Parallel Imaging (PI) and Compressed Sensing (CS), tend to introduce substantial noise and blurring when pushed to high acceleration factors. Although they rely on fundamentally different redundancies, combining them synergistically remains an open challenge. METHODS: The GoLF-SPARKLING framework was extended to jointly exploit two acceleration mechanisms: PI-based uniform undersampling in the central k-space region and variable-density CS at the periphery, with independent acceleration factors in each zone. To preserve smooth signal evolution throughout the inversion-recovery period and avoid modulation artifacts, the acquisition trajectory was reordered accordingly. The resulting method was evaluated prospectively in vivo at 1 mm isotropic resolution and benchmarked against Wave-CAIPI and Poisson-disk sampling as respective PI and CS baselines. RESULTS: The proposed hybrid approach produced sharper, less noisy, and more stable whole-brain images in approximately 1 min than either acceleration strategy alone. Purely PI-based reconstructions were degraded by high g-factor noise, while exclusively CS-based reconstructions exhibited pronounced blurring. Furthermore, this method yielded lower average volumetric errors in downstream automated brain segmentation than state-of-the-art acceleration techniques, demonstrating its clinical utility. CONCLUSION: By jointly leveraging PI and CS, GoLF-SPARKLING achieves high acceleration factors that enable sub-minute, high-quality anatomical MRI. This translates into greater clinical throughput and more reliable imaging in patients who are challenging to scan.

articles.title: Reduced Hippocampal Subfield Volumes in Neonates with Low 1-Minute Apgar Scores Correlate with Umbilical Artery Blood Gas Parameters.
articles.abstract: OBJECTIVE: Perinatal asphyxia may induce brain injury, while the effects of transient hypoxia on hippocampal subregions remain unclear. Using the 1-minute Apgar score, this study examined its effects on hippocampal volumes and correlations with umbilical artery blood gas parameters (UABG), providing imaging evidence to evaluate hypoxia-related brain injury. METHODS: Neonates were assigned to the low Apgar score (LAS) group and the normal Apgar score (NAS) group. All subjects underwent 3D T1-weighted brain MRI for hippocampal volumetry. UABG indices, including pH, lactate (LAC), and base excess (BE), were collected. We performed an analysis of covariance with sex, postmenstrual age at MRI, and total brain volume as covariates, followed by correlation analysis. RESULTS: Multiple hippocampal subfields exhibited significantly smaller volumes in the LAS group (all FDR-corrected q < 0.05). Within-group analyses identified correlations between hippocampal volumes and UABG parameters. In the LAS group, left parasubiculum volume was correlated with pH and base excess, and in the NAS group, left parasubiculum volume correlated with the two indicators, while right tail volume correlated with pH. CONCLUSION: Neonates with lower 1-minute Apgar scores exhibit reduced volume of specific hippocampal subregions, correlating with umbilical artery blood gas parameters. These findings link transiently low 1-minute Apgar scores with hippocampal subregional morphology during the neonatal period. ADVANCES IN KNOWLEDGE: We investigated neonates with low 1-minute Apgar scores that normalized at 5 minutes and found their hippocampal subregional structural changes correlated with umbilical artery blood gas parameters.

articles.title: Spatial coupling between anosmia-related cortical alterations and regional gene expression: an imaging transcriptomics study.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: The impact of anosmia on brain cortical structure and the underlying molecular mechanisms remain unclear. This study investigated causal associations between anosmia and cortical alterations using a multi-modal approach combining neuroimaging and genetics. METHODS: High-resolution structural magnetic resonance imaging was acquired from 52 patients with anosmia and 50 healthy controls to extract cortical surface area (SA) and cortical thickness (TH). Mendelian randomization (MR) was employed to assess the causal effect of anosmia on cortical structure using summary statistics from the ENIGMA consortium. Furthermore, integrating gene expression data from the Allen Human Brain Atlas (AHBA), partial least squares regression (PLSR) and summary-data-based Mendelian randomization (SMR) were used to identify genes associated with changes in SA and TH due to anosmia. Gene enrichment analysis and cell type-specific analysis were then performed to explore the potential molecular mechanisms. RESULTS: Patients exhibited significantly reduced SA in the left rostral anterior cingulate and superior temporal sulcus, while TH was increased in regions including the left cuneus and supramarginal gyrus. MR analysis identified 11 cortical structural features nominally associated with anosmia, although none survived multiple comparison correction across 138 tests. Transcriptomic analysis identified genes correlated with these structural alterations, which were significantly enriched in synaptic pathways (e.g., postsynaptic membrane modulation) and specifically implicated GABAergic and glutamatergic neurons. CONCLUSION: Anosmia is causally associated with distinct cortical structural alterations. These regional changes are spatially coupled with molecular signatures involving synaptic function and neuronal plasticity, providing novel insights into the potential pathophysiology of olfactory loss.

articles.title: Bioabsorbable spacer-assisted high-dose proton beam therapy for unresectable locally advanced pancreatic cancer of the body or tail: a feasibility and safety study.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND AND PURPOSE: Anatomical proximity to gastrointestinal (GI) organs can preclude dose-escalated irradiation for locally advanced pancreatic cancer (LAPC). We evaluated the safety and feasibility of bioabsorbable spacer-assisted high-dose proton beam therapy (PBT) for unresectable LAPC of the pancreatic body or tail. MATERIALS AND METHODS: This exploratory retrospective analysis used retrospectively reviewed perioperative data and retrospectively or prospectively collected PBT data. Fourteen patients with presumed nonmetastatic LAPC underwent placement of a bioabsorbable polyglycolic acid (PGA) spacer. Thirteen received definitive PBT at 67.5 or 75 Gy (relative biological effectiveness [RBE]) in 25 fractions. The composite primary safety endpoint was the occurrence of a Clavien-Dindo grade ≥III surgical complication or a CTCAE grade ≥3 adverse event related to definitive PBT or concurrent chemotherapy. RESULTS: Spacer placement achieved ≥10 mm tumor-GI separation in all 14 patients; 13 completed definitive PBT. No Clavien-Dindo grade ≥III surgical complication occurred. Four of 13 definitive-PBT patients (30.8%) experienced at least one qualifying safety event: one experienced grade 3 nausea and three other patients experienced grade 3 leukopenia/neutropenia. No grade ≥3 structural GI injury was observed. Median follow-up was 19.3 months. Median overall and progression-free survival were 24.8 and 11.8 months, respectively; 1- and 2-year local control rates were 81.5% and 38.2%. CONCLUSION: Bioabsorbable spacer-assisted high-dose PBT was technically feasible in this selected cohort. However, this small, uncontrolled study cannot establish a low risk of uncommon or late adverse events or support conclusions regarding comparative safety or efficacy.

articles.title: Independent validation of a predictive risk model for contrast-enhancing brain lesions supports enhanced periventricular radiosensitivity and variable proton RBE.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND AND PURPOSE: Contrast-enhancing brain lesions (CEBLs) were reported as MR-imaging (MRI) endpoint to assess dose effects in healthy brain tissue following proton radiotherapy (PRT) of low-grade-glioma (LGG) patients. A voxel-level risk model was proposed with absorbed dose (D), dose-averaged linear energy transfer (LETD), and proximity to the ventricular system as risk factors. We validated this model in an independent LGG patient cohort. MATERIAL AND METHODS: LGG patients treated at the same institution but more recently (2015-2019) were considered. For each patient, follow-up MRI data were screened for CEBLs, complication-risk maps were calculated and patient-level NTCPCEBL values were determined according to the original model. Eventually, risk model coefficients were updated by regressing the original logistic model to the validation cohort (validC) data. RESULTS: The validC comprised 112 subjects. Observed CEBL incidence of 21% was the same as in the modelling cohort (modelC); observed number of CEBLs and median lesion volume were considerably smaller in the validC, (NvalidC = 26, NmodelC = 67 and Vmed,validC = 110 mm3, Vmed,modelC = 235 mm3). Good calibration of the original patient-level NTCPCEBL model was obtained in the validC. Update of the model coefficients yielded a more pronounced LETD-effect and a 2.4 times higher odds ratio for the complication risk in the periventricular space (PVS). CONCLUSIONS: The presented validation confirms an enhanced radiosensitivity of the PVS, a variable proton RBE, and supports serial complication characteristics of the brain. This underlines the need for a PRT strategy that actively spares the PVS under consideration of an LETD-dependent proton RBE. CLINICAL TRIAL INFORMATION: The study was approved by the ethics committee of the Heidelberg University Hospital (ethics vote: S-516/2022).

articles.title: Phase I dose-escalation study of stereotactic body radiotherapy with elective nodal irradiation for borderline resectable and unresectable locally advanced pancreatic cancer.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Locoregional recurrence remains a major clinical challenge in borderline resectable (BR) and unresectable locally advanced (UR-LA) pancreatic cancer, even after stereotactic body radiotherapy (SBRT). This phase I trial evaluated the safety, maximum tolerated dose (MTD), and preliminary efficacy of adding prophylactic elective nodal irradiation (ENI) to 5-fraction SBRT. METHODS: Patients with BR/UR-LAPC were enrolled in a 3 + 3 dose-escalation design. SBRT was delivered in 5 fractions using either adaptive magnetic resonance image-guided radiation therapy or respiratory breath-hold radiotherapy with a fiducial marker. The ENI dose was fixed at 30 Gy in five fractions, while the primary tumor dose increased from Level 1 (35 Gy) to Level 3 (40 Gy). The primary endpoint was acute dose-limiting toxicity (DLT) (any Grade ≥ 3 non-hematological adverse events within 14 days after the completion of SBRT). RESULTS: Twelve patients (BR: 4, LA: 8) were enrolled, 11 of whom had previously received systemic chemotherapy. One patient at Level 1 experienced acute Grade 3 anorexia/nausea requiring hospitalization. No DLTs were observed at Levels 2 and 3, and the MTD was not reached. Three patients with preexisting biliary stents developed subacute Grade 3 cholangitis. No Grade ≥ 3 late adverse events occurred. The median overall survival after SBRT was 17.3 months, and the 1-year locoregional control rate was 75%. CONCLUSION: Five-fraction SBRT with simultaneous 30 Gy ENI was feasible, and the MTD was not reached within the tested dose levels up to 40 Gy. Further prospective studies are needed to evaluate its long-term safety and treatment outcomes.

articles.title: Clinical value of 18F-FDG PET/CT for detecting residual metastatic lymph nodes of DTC before initial radioiodine therapy.
articles.abstract: OBJECTIVE: To evaluate the adjunctive value of 18F-FDG PET/CT for assessing residual metastatic lymph nodes (MLN) before initial radioiodine therapy in postoperative DTC patients with high clinical suspicion of residual nodal disease. METHODS: This retrospective study included 835 postoperative patients with DTC who underwent 18F-FDG PET/CT before initial 131I therapy because of elevated stimulated thyroglobulin (sTg) and/or suspicious conventional neck imaging. MLN status was determined using a composite reference standard. Patient-level logistic regression was used to evaluate associated factors, and receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analysis was performed to assess discrimination and determine optimal cutoffs. A sensitivity analysis reassessed diagnostic performance using a reference assessment that excluded PET/CT information. RESULTS: Of the 835 patients, 452 (54.1%) were classified as having residual MLN. Under the composite reference standard, PET/CT showed a sensitivity of 84.5% and a specificity of 73.4%. After PET/CT information was excluded from the reference assessment, 104 patients were classified as indeterminate; among the remaining 731 patients, sensitivity remained similar at 85.9%, whereas specificity decreased to 40.1%. PET/CT contributed to N-stage revision in 149/835 (17.8%) patients, including a joint contribution with conventional imaging in 129 patients and an independent incremental contribution in 20 patients. Among patients with residual MLN, 275/452 (60.8%) exhibited an FDG-avid/131I-nonavid pattern. In TgAb-negative patients, multivariable analysis showed that nodal maximum standardized uptake value (SUVmax) and sTg were independently associated with residual MLN (both P < 0.001). The corresponding ROC-derived cutoffs were 4.6 and 14.58 µg/L, respectively. CONCLUSIONS: In postoperative DTC patients with a high clinical suspicion of residual nodal disease, 18F-FDG PET/CT may complement conventional imaging and biochemical assessment in identifying residual MLN and refining N-stage assessment.

articles.title: Carotid CTA with automated plaque quantification for risk stratification of coexisting obstructive coronary artery disease.
articles.abstract: OBJECTIVES: To evaluate whether automated carotid plaque quantification on carotid computed tomography angiography (CTA) can serve as an adjunctive risk stratification tool for identifying patients with coexisting obstructive coronary artery disease (OCAD). MATERIALS AND METHODS: This dual-center retrospective study included 2533 adults undergoing paired carotid and coronary CTA within 3 months. Carotid plaque components (calcified, fibrotic, and lipid) were quantified automatically. In the modeling cohort, three diagnostic models for OCAD (stenosis ≥ 50%) were developed using LASSO regression: clinical, plaque, and integrated models. Performance was assessed by AUC (with DeLong's test), decision curve analysis, and calibration curves, with validation in an internal validation set and a temporally independent validation cohort. Sensitivity analysis was performed using severe stenosis (≥ 70%) as the outcome. RESULTS: All carotid plaque volumes were significantly associated with OCAD (p < 0.001). Calcified plaque volume (OR, 2.43; 95% CI: 1.95-3.04) and fibrotic plaque volume (OR, 1.37; 95% CI: 1.01-1.85) were independent predictors. The plaque model achieved an AUC of 0.785 (95% CI: 0.761-0.810) in the training set, comparable to the integrated model (AUC, 0.800) and superior to the clinical model (AUC, 0.723; p < 0.001). Performance remained robust in the internal (AUC, 0.824) and external validation set (AUC, 0.813). The integrated model demonstrated good calibration. Sensitivity analysis yielded consistent results. CONCLUSION: In this retrospective study, automated carotid plaque quantification on CTA provides an adjunctive risk stratification tool to identify patients at high risk for coexisting OCAD, potentially guiding decisions regarding downstream coronary examinations. KEY POINTS: Question Quantitative analysis of carotid plaque components on CTA may help identify patients with OCAD. Findings A model integrating automated carotid plaque volumes and clinical factors effectively identified OCAD. Clinical Relevance This study demonstrates that automated carotid plaque quantification on CTA may serve as an adjunctive risk stratification tool to guide downstream coronary testing in patients with cerebrovascular disease.

articles.title: Multidimensional Neural Maturity Indices from Naturalistic fMRI Reveal the Longitudinal Development of Theory of Mind.
articles.abstract: Theory of Mind (ToM) develops from early reasoning about others' beliefs and intentions toward more advanced forms of recursive and socially embedded mental-state understanding. This ability emerges alongside the progressive maturation of large-scale brain networks. Here, we introduce a multidimensional neural maturity framework, derived from naturalistic functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI), that characterizes children's neurofunctional maturation along three dimensions: functional connectivity, temporal fluctuation, and spatial activation, by capturing neural responses to social narratives. Using an accelerated longitudinal design (baseline ages 3-9 years; 27-30-month follow-up), we applied this framework to examine how social-cognitive brain networks mature across complementary dimensions of brain function and how such maturation relates to ToM development. Across childhood, all three neural indices increased longitudinally, indicating progressive maturation of social-cognitive networks. Brain-behavior analyses further highlighted temporal fluctuation and spatial activation maturity as dimensions most closely related to ToM performance. Longitudinal path models indicated developmental continuity from elementary to advanced ToM, and suggested that advanced mental-state reasoning develops in coordination with the multidimensional longitudinal maturation of social-cognitive neural responses. Together, these findings provide initial longitudinal neurodevelopmental evidence that children's social-cognitive networks become increasingly adult-like across multiple neurofunctional dimension, offering a neurodevelopmental extension of behavioral accounts of the transition from elementary to advanced mental-state reasoning.

articles.title: Incidence of fractures after cryoablation of sclerotic or mixed-type metastases in the spine and pelvis without concurrent consolidation.
articles.abstract: PURPOSE: To evaluate the incidence of secondary fractures after cryoablation of sclerotic or mixed-type metastases in the spine and pelvis without concurrent consolidation, and to identify associated risk factors. MATERIALS AND METHODS: A retrospective single-center analysis of 66 sclerotic or mixed-type metastases in the vertebral column or pelvis in 55 patients (median age 59 years, 45% men) treated with percutaneous cryoablation without simultaneous consolidation between 2018 and 2026 was performed. Follow-up cross-sectional imaging was assessed for evidence of fracture, and univariable logistic regression analysis was performed to identify patient-specific, procedural and radiographic characteristics associated with fracture occurrence. Candidate cut-offs were explored by ROC analysis. RESULTS: Over a median follow-up of 13 months, six fractures (9%) occurred in the treated area after a mean delay of 4.7 months (range 1-9 months). Five of six patients (83%) were symptomatic, and 4/6 (67%) required subsequent consolidation. Metastasis size (OR=1.32 per cm increase, 95% CI 1.01-1.75; p=0.046) and the number of cryoprobes (OR=2.93, CI 1.61-6.49; p<0.001) were significantly associated with fracture occurrence. In a sensitivity analysis restricted to one lesion per patient, the association with cryoprobe number remained robust, whereas that with size was attenuated. Exploratory cut-offs were 4 cryoprobes (AUC 0.846) and 5.8 cm (0.749). CONCLUSION: Isolated cryoablation of sclerotic or mixed-type metastases in the spine and pelvis carries an estimated fracture risk of ∼9%, increasing with metastasis size and the number of cryoprobes used. These findings may aid risk stratification and help to identify which patients could benefit from additional consolidation.

articles.title: A novel image-domain denoising method for triple-material decomposition in dual-energy CT.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Triple-material decomposition (TMD) holds significant clinical value in dual-energy computed tomography (DECT), as it enables simultaneous differentiation of bone, soft tissue, and contrast agents-three key components commonly targeted in clinical imaging assessments. However, the inherent noise amplification artifact associated with material decomposition remains a critical technical bottleneck that restricts its widespread clinical translation. PURPOSE: To address this limitation, this study proposes an image-domain denoising strategy to mitigate noise amplification, thereby improving the quantitative accuracy and qualitative quality of TMD in DECT. METHOD: First, DECT images were transformed into amplitude and argument components via vectorization. Second, a spectral joint bilateral filtering algorithm was developed to specifically denoise the argument images, leveraging inter-spectral correlation to preserve structural details while suppressing noise. Subsequently, denoised DECT images were reconstructed using the original amplitude and denoised argument components. TMD was performed with soft tissue, bone, and contrast agent as basis materials, utilizing two decomposition approaches: direct matrix inversion (DMI) and the penalized weighted least squares-expectation maximization-loop (PWLS-EP-LOOP) iterative method. The proposed denoising strategy was validated on a benchtop micro-CT system, with evaluations conducted on both a customized anthropomorphic phantom and an in vivo mouse model injected with ExiTron nano 6000 contrast agent. RESULTS: For DMI-based decomposition, the proposed method achieved noise reduction rates (NRRs) of 68.9% in soft tissue images, 74.4% in contrast-enhanced images, and 78.7% in bone images. For PWLS-EP-LOOP-based iterative decomposition, the corresponding NRRs were 22.4% (soft tissue), 48.6% (contrast agent), and 37.5% (bone). Furthermore, the number of iteration cycles required for convergence in the PWLS-EP-LOOP algorithm was reduced by 75.4%, substantially improving computational efficiency. CONCLUSION: Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed image-domain denoising method, tailored for DECT TMD, effectively suppresses noise in both DMI and iterative workflows while preserving structural fidelity. This work thus provides a promising solution to enhance the clinical utility of DECT material decomposition.

articles.title: A K-space guided invertible diffusion model for accelerating MRI reconstruction.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), a core technology in clinical medical diagnosis, has long aimed to balance imaging quality and acquisition efficiency. Traditional MRI techniques, limited by the Nyquist-Shannon sampling theorem, are faced with significant challenges in high-acceleration-factor imaging, including artifacts and detail loss due to sparse sampling. While existing parallel imaging, compressed sensing, and deep learning methods have improved reconstruction efficiency, they have limitations such as insufficient integration of electromagnetic physics models with biological tissue prior information, inadequate high-frequency information recovery, and high computational complexity. PURPOSE: To address these persistent limitations in high-acceleration MRI reconstruction, this study proposes a K-space guided invertible diffusion model (KG-IDM) designed to improve reconstruction fidelity. METHODS: KG-IDM enables high-quality MRI reconstruction through Cross-domain Feature Injection (CFI) with Adaptive Channel-Spatial Interaction Attention (ACSIA) for multi-source feature alignment, and a K-space Guided Bimodal Spectral Enhancement Network (KG-BSEN) for dual-path frequency-spatial enhancement. This framework jointly exploits spatial and spectral representations, enhancing cross-domain feature consistency and reducing reconstruction artifacts. RESULTS: Experiments on the fastMRI single-coil knee dataset using retrospectively undersampled complex-valued k-space at 4 ×  , 6 ×  , 8 ×  , and 10 ×  acceleration show that KG-IDM achieves the highest mean PSNR and SSIM and the lowest mean NMSE relative to all nine baseline methods. At 4 ×  acceleration, KG-IDM achieves 32.05   dB PSNR, 81.35 %  SSIM, and 0.0230  NMSE. At 10 ×  , it achieves 25.58   dB, 62.55 %  , and 0.0815  , respectively. Paired volume-level Wilcoxon tests over 199 evaluation volumes showed statistically significant favorable differences in all 108 comparisons, with all Holm-adjusted p < 10 - 4    . CONCLUSIONS: By integrating measurement-guided cross-domain feature fusion with frequency-spatial refinement, KG-IDM consistently improves reconstruction fidelity across the evaluated acceleration factors and provides a promising framework for accelerated MRI reconstruction.

articles.title: Advancing cyber-physical systems in surgery through a smart cyber operating theater testbed for medical device integration and clinical translation.
articles.abstract: PURPOSE: Operating-room devices and robotic systems are often standalone, which limits synchronized multi-source data utilization and cyber-physical surgical support. This Short Communication presents an integration approach for a Smart Cyber Operating Theater (SCOT) based on OPeLiNK, and reports log-based operational reliability in a clinical SCOT environment. Our focus is the architecture and feasibility of time-synchronized data integration rather than clinical outcome evaluation. METHODS: OPeLiNK was implemented as a common interface and integration architecture consisting of device-specific providers, a data server for management and time synchronization, and application-level data distribution. A university SCOT testbed was established in 2016 for onboarding and integration verification without interrupting clinical workflow. Operational reliability was assessed using de-identified integration logs collected in the clinical SCOT environment (HyperSCOT), defining a successful session as meeting all criteria: required device connection, data reception, application-level display, and time synchronization. RESULTS: The SCOT testbed enabled integration across heterogeneous connections (e.g., Ethernet, serial communication, USB, and video outputs) and supported verification of interconnectivity, including communication validation, data structure consistency, and behavior under abnormal termination and restart. As an application example, a Surgical Strategy Desk was demonstrated using simulated/demo data to show synchronized multi-source visualization. In the clinical environment, SCOT has been used since 2019, including at least 437 glioma surgeries, providing real-world operational logs to support the log-based reliability assessment. CONCLUSIONS: We present an OPeLiNK-based SCOT integration approach and a testbed framework for safe onboarding and verification, complemented by log-based operational evidence from clinical use since 2019. Although clinical effectiveness and efficiency outcomes are out of scope for this Short Communication, reliable time-synchronized integration is a necessary foundation for future cyber-physical operating theaters and advanced decision support applications.
articles.journal: Int J Comput Assist Radiol Surg

articles.title: Bias-corrected respiratory motion standard deviation from amplitude-binned 4D-MRI for radiotherapy planning.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Respiratory-resolved magnetic resonance imaging (4D-MRI) provides superior soft-tissue contrast for characterizing respiratory motion in radiotherapy, but its geometric fidelity depends on the reconstruction and binning strategy. As with 4D-CT, peak-to-peak amplitude derived from binned 4D-MRI is prone to underestimation. However, as acquisitions span many respiratory cycles, the standard deviation (SD) of motion, required for probability-based planning approaches such as mid-ventilation, may be estimated accurately, provided binning-induced bias is corrected. PURPOSE: To develop and validate a motion SD estimator for equal-probability amplitude-binned 4D-MRI data that corrects for systematic underestimation caused by intra-bin motion variability. METHODS: 4D-MRI data were acquired on a dynamic motion phantom driven by five patient-derived respiratory traces. Images were reconstructed using both a standard non-uniform fast Fourier transform (NUFFT) and the compressed sensing-based XD-GRASP algorithm with varying numbers (2-20) of equal-probability respiratory amplitude bins. An SD estimator based on the law of total variance was implemented to correct for intra-bin variance. The accuracy of peak-to-peak amplitude and SD was evaluated against ground-truth physical phantom motion, with performance under deformable motion tested on a digital phantom (CoMBAT). RESULTS: Both reconstruction methods underestimated true peak-to-peak motion. While the inter-bin SD calculation also underestimated motion variability, the proposed correction substantially mitigated this bias. It yielded robust SD estimates with median residual underestimation of 0.13 mm (5 bins) and 0.11 mm (10 bins) across patient traces. In CoMBAT, the absolute bias of the total SD estimate was below 3% from five bins onward. CONCLUSIONS: The proposed estimator provides an accurate measurement of respiratory motion SD from amplitude-binned 4D-MRI by accounting for intra-bin variability. This supports the reliability of 4D-MRI for planning strategies dependent on motion probability distributions. Additionally, the confirmed underestimation of peak-to-peak amplitude highlights a fundamental limitation in defining internal target volumes directly from binned 4D-MRI.

articles.title: Beyond chronological age: uncovering disease-dependent variability in AI-driven pediatric bone age assessment.
articles.abstract: OBJECTIVES: To assess performance and agreement of a commercial artificial intelligence (AI) tool relative to routine pediatric radiologists' bone age assessments in a large pediatric cohort, with focus on different groups of growth disorders. MATERIALS AND METHODS: One thousand five hundred sixteen anterior-posterior hand radiographs of pediatric patients (50.6% boys, mean age 10.84 ± 3.66 years) were retrospectively analyzed using the AI tool BoneAge. AI results were compared with board-certified pediatric radiologists' reports using Bland-Altman plots, Spearman correlations, and the intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC). Subgroup analyses were performed for three major indications: genetic/neuroendocrine (n = 1179), orthopedic (n = 152), and oncologic disorders (n = 185). RESULTS: Mean absolute difference (MAD) in estimated bone age by radiologists and AI was 6.4 ± 7.0 months for the whole cohort, with complete concordance in 45.1% of cases. Best results were achieved in orthopedic questions with an MAD of 4.1 ± 5.6 months (genetic/neuroendocrine: 6.6 ± 7.2, oncologic: 6.7 ± 6.3 months). There was significant correlation between AI and radiologists for the whole study population (ρ = 0.980), and the three main groups: genetic/neuroendocrine (ρ = 0.974), orthopedic (ρ = 0.952), and oncologic indications (ρ = 0.988). ICCs for the entire cohort and the main indication groups were > 0.9, indicating excellent agreement between radiologist and AI. CONCLUSION: The investigated algorithm showed good agreement with bone age assessments performed by pediatric radiologists in a large pediatric cohort. Novel to previous studies, the indication for imaging was considered, demonstrating that agreement between algorithm output and radiologists' assessments varied across disease groups, with highest agreement observed in orthopedic indications. KEY POINTS: Question The performance of artificial intelligence tools for bone age assessment among different subgroups of pediatric patients according to underlying diseases has not yet been investigated. Findings Automated bone age assessment reliably correlates with estimation by pediatric radiologists. Software output differs according to disease groups, with best results for orthopedic indications. Critical relevance statement In a real-world scenario, the commercial software showed good agreement with routine bone age assessments in a large cohort of pediatric patients. The observed disease-dependent variation suggests that radiologists should consider disease-specific differences when using additional automated tools.

articles.title: Structural brain changes in age-related macular degeneration before and 6 months after Scharioth macula lens implantation: an exploratory MRI study.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND AND PURPOSE: Age-related macular degeneration (AMD) is associated with visual impairment and with structural and functional brain differences. The extent of these differences and whether longitudinal structural changes are detectable after visual rehabilitation, including implantation of the Scharioth macula lens (SML), remain incompletely understood. This study aimed primarily to characterize baseline deviations from normative MRI reference values and secondarily to describe whether longitudinal changes were detectable after SML implantation. MATERIALS AND METHODS: Ten patients with dry AMD (mean age 78.8 ± 5.6 years) underwent structural brain MRI at 3 T before and 6 months after SML implantation. Regional volumes and age-, sex-, and head-size-normalized normative percentiles were generated using the fully automated AI-assisted multi-atlas segmentation tool (cNeuro cMRI). All reported hypothesis tests used normative percentiles; absolute regional volumes were not used in inferential analyses. Analyses included baseline deviation in an anatomically defined visual-network family (k = 36), exploratory longitudinal visual-network tests (k = 36), an exploratory analysis outside that network (k = 221), and an exploratory reduced-dimension family of three brain and three quality-of-life (VFQ-25) composites (k = 6), with false discovery rate (FDR) correction within each family. RESULTS: At baseline, deviation from the normative median survived FDR correction for the left, total, and right occipital pole and the left lingual gyrus. Longitudinal visual-network observations were limited to uncorrected exploratory changes in the left middle occipital gyrus (p = 0.004, pFDR = 0.141), total occipital pole (p = 0.027, pFDR = 0.428), and left occipital lobe (p = 0.049, pFDR = 0.428); none survived FDR correction. No region outside the visual network survived FDR correction (minimum pFDR = 0.216). None of the six reduced-dimension composites survived FDR correction, and no exploratory structure-function association or regression coefficient was robust after correction or interval estimation. CONCLUSIONS: Patients with dry AMD showed regionally selective structural deviations in the posterior visual cortex, particularly the occipital pole, relative to the normative MRI reference. No longitudinal finding within or outside the visual network survived FDR correction; the uncorrected regional observations were heterogeneous and are considered exploratory. Because the study was sensitive only to large within-subject effects, the absence of corrected structural change should be interpreted in the context of limited sensitivity and not as evidence that structural change was absent.

articles.title: Tumor-masked structural connectomics for assessing tract-specific white matter disruption associated with glioma aggressiveness: an interpretable machine learning pilot study.
articles.abstract: PURPOSE: To assess the feasibility of personalized tumor-masked structural connectomics combined with interpretable machine learning (ML) for differentiating low-grade gliomas (LGG) from high-grade gliomas (HGG), and to identify candidate tract-specific connectomic biomarkers of glioma aggressiveness. METHODS: Thirty-five patients with histopathologically confirmed gliomas (20 LGG, 15 HGG) underwent preoperative diffusion tensor imaging and T1-weighted MRI. Tumor-masked probabilistic tractography was used to reconstruct individualized structural connectomes based on 50 white matter (WM) tract labels. We evaluated 296 graph-theoretical features using sequential feature selection and Random Forest classification within a strictly isolated nested cross-validation framework. We used SHAP analysis for model interpretation. Sensitivity analyses compared clinical-radiological, connectomic, and combined feature sets. RESULTS: The leak-free pure connectomics model achieved a mean ROC-AUC of 0.814 ± 0.327 (95% CI, 0.500-1.000), with a macro-F1 score of 0.786 ± 0.265. Restricting the analysis to non-zero connectomic features yielded a mean AUC of 0.833 ± 0.167. The clinical-radiological model achieved a mean AUC of 0.817 ± 0.149, while the combined clinical-radiological and connectomic model showed the highest point estimate (AUC, 0.933 ± 0.109; 95% CI, 0.798-1.068). SHAP analysis highlighted the sagittal stratum, medial lemniscus, and superior fronto-occipital fasciculus among the most informative WM pathways. CONCLUSION: Tumor-masked structural connectomics combined with interpretable ML demonstrated preliminary feasibility for identifying candidate imaging biomarkers associated with glioma aggressiveness in neuroradiological practice. These findings are exploratory and represent internal estimates from a single cohort; external validation in independent, multi-center cohorts is required before any potential clinical application.

articles.title: MRI Radiomics and Deep Learning for Differentiating Spinal Tuberculosis from Spinal Metastasis: A Multicenter Study.
articles.abstract: OBJECTIVES: To develop radiomics model, 2D deep learning (2D DL) model, 2.5D deep learning (2.5D DL) model, 3D deep learning (3D DL) model, and their fusion models to differentiate spinal tuberculosis (STB) from spinal metastasis (SM) based on MR imaging. METHODS: This retrospective study included 186 STB patients and 219 SM patients. Patients from three hospitals were divided into a training set (n = 191), an internal test set (n = 82) and an external test set (n = 132). Using the ResNet50 network pre-trained leveraging the ImageNet dataset, we developed 2D, 2.5D, and 3D deep learning models based on MR imaging. We constructed the radiomics model by using PyRadiomics to extract radiomics features. Deep learning models and radiomics model were used to construct two fusion models: the feature-based model (Rad_DL_FB) and the decision-based model (Rad_DL_DB). And the accuracy of these models was validated. RESULTS: In the internal test set, the Rad_DL_FB model demonstrated superior performance compared to other models, achieving the highest AUC of 0.971 (95% CI: 0.953-0.989) and accuracy of 0.927. In the external test set, the Rad_DL_DB model demonstrated superior performance compared to other models, achieving the highest AUC of 0.961 (95% CI: 0.940-0.982) and accuracy of 0.909. Furthermore, fusion-model assistance significantly improved the diagnostic accuracy of junior spine surgeons and narrowed the observed performance gap between junior and senior surgeons. CONCLUSION: The fusion models including Rad_DL_FB model and Rad_DL_DB model, which integrates radiomics features and deep learning features of different dimensions, can effectively differentiate STB from SM, thereby assisting clinicians in making clinical decisions.

articles.title: Construction and Validation of a Prediction Model for TACE Resistance in Hepatocellular Carcinoma Based on Contrast-Enhanced Ultrasound Radiomics.
articles.abstract: OBJECTIVE: To construct and validate a contrast-enhanced ultrasound (CEUS) radiomics-clinical model for predicting transarterial chemoembolization (TACE) resistance in hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC). METHODS: A total of 168 HCC patients who underwent CEUS on two vendor platforms (Philips E9 and GE Logiq E95) were split into a training set (n = 118) and an internal validation set (n = 50), with an additional 80 patients forming an external validation cohort. For each patient, 2D regions of interest were manually delineated on the largest cross-sectional slice of each CEUS phase. Radiomic features were extracted and screened by LASSO regression; the twelve retained features were linearly combined into a single Rad-score. The Rad-score and three prespecified clinical risk factors (tumor size, Child-Pugh class, AFP) confirmed by multivariate analysis were combined into a parsimonious logistic regression (LR) model with four predictors in total. Performance was assessed by ROC curve, calibration curve, decision curve analysis (DCA), subgroup analysis, and prospective validation. RESULTS: The combined model had AUCs of 0.895, 0.891 and 0.846 in three sets, with subgroup AUCs >0.86. Prospective validation showed TACE plus sorafenib improved 6-month response rate from 26.7% to 53.3% for high-risk patients. CONCLUSION: The CEUS radiomics-clinical model accurately predicts TACE resistance, guiding individualized HCC treatment. ADVANCES IN KNOWLEDGE: This model integrates CEUS multi-phase radiomics and clinical factors, outperforming single clinical/radiomic models. Strict multi-step screening and comprehensive validation avoid data leakage, ensuring robust prediction and clinical translatability.

articles.title: Brenner Tumors of the Ovary: Spectrum of Sonographic Findings: A Systematic Review.
articles.abstract: The objective of the study is to systematically review the literature on the clinical and sonographic features of ovarian Brenner tumors (BTs) and identify characteristics potentially associated with benign versus borderline or malignant histology. PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, and Web of Science were systematically searched for studies reporting sonographic findings in histologically confirmed ovarian BTs published between January 2000 and November 2025. Findings were summarized descriptively, and exploratory comparisons were performed between benign Brenner tumors (BBTs) and borderline or malignant BTs. Twenty-six studies (19 case reports and 7 case series) involving 150 tumors in 133 patients were included. Of the tumors, 110 were benign and 40 were borderline (n = 9) or malignant (n = 31). Most tumors contained a solid component (78.0%). Tumor morphology differed between groups (p = .012), and solid components were more frequent in borderline or malignant tumors than in benign tumors (90.0% versus 73.6%; p = .044). Moderate or abundant vascularity was more frequent in borderline or malignant tumors (75.8% versus 28.9%; p < .001), whereas acoustic shadowing was more frequent in benign tumors (75.8% versus 11.4%; p < .001). Calcifications or hyperechoic areas occurred at similar frequencies (58.3% versus 50.0%; p = .434). Ovarian BTs appear to exhibit 2 partially contrasting sonographic phenotypes. Benign tumors are commonly solid, poorly vascularized masses with prominent acoustic shadowing, whereas borderline or malignant tumors tend to show greater morphologic complexity, increased vascularity, and less acoustic shadowing. Vascularity and acoustic shadowing may be useful in preoperative characterization, but prospective studies using standardized ultrasound terminology are needed to validate these observations.

articles.title: Virtual non-calcium dual-energy computed tomography for postoperative lumbar spine evaluation following pedicle screw instrumentation.
articles.abstract: PURPOSE: To compare standard grayscale CT, 140-keV virtual monoenergetic imaging, and virtual non-calcium (VNCa) for detection of magnetic resonance imaging (MRI)-defined relevant foraminal stenosis, disc protrusion or extrusion, and relevant nerve root compression. METHODS: This retrospective study included patients who underwent dual-energy computed tomography (DECT) on a 128-slice single-tube system and MRI within 1 week between August and December 2025; CT reconstructions were read in consensus. Foraminal stenosis and nerve root compression grades 2-3 were considered imaging-defined relevant findings. Only segments with an MRI confidence score of 5 were included. Diagnostic performance and CT confidence scores were summarized descriptively. RESULTS: Twenty-three patients (mean age, 60 ± 12 years; 15 women) contributed 185 evaluated segments. MRI showed relevant foraminal stenosis in 26 segments and disc protrusion or extrusion and relevant nerve root compression in 18 segments each. Foraminal-stenosis sensitivity was 100.0% (26/26) for VNCa and 92.3% (24/26) for both comparators; specificity was 88.7%, 71.1%, and 72.3% for VNCa, standard CT, and 140-keV CT, respectively. Disc protrusion or extrusion sensitivity was 77.8% (14/18) for VNCa and 11.1% (2/18) for both comparators. Standard CT and VNCa each had 83.3% sensitivity and 97.0% specificity for nerve root compression. CONCLUSION: In this small, selected cohort, VNCa had higher observed specificity for MRI-defined foraminal stenosis and higher observed sensitivity for disc protrusion or extrusion. These exploratory findings require confirmation in larger studies that account for patient-level clustering and include more artifact-limited examinations. CLINICAL SIGNIFICANCE: VNCa reconstruction from an existing DECT examination may complement grayscale CT for evaluating MRI-defined foraminal stenosis and disc protrusion or extrusion following lumbar pedicle screw instrumentation without requiring additional scanning.

articles.title: Association of baseline chest computed tomography (CT) findings with inpatient sputum smear positivity and grade in active pulmonary tuberculosis: a retrospective study.
articles.abstract: AIM: In adults admitted with active pulmonary tuberculosis (TB), smear positivity and grade are practical markers of bacillary burden but may be unavailable during early inpatient assessment. We assessed whether baseline chest computed tomography (CT) findings were associated with smear positivity and higher grade. MATERIALS AND METHODS: We performed a single-centre retrospective study of adults with active pulmonary TB who underwent chest CT within 7 days of admission and sputum smear microscopy within 48 hours. Structured CT variables were extracted, and inter-reader agreement was assessed in a dual-reader subset. Outcomes were smear positivity and ordinal smear grade (Negative, Scanty, 1+, 2+, or 3+). Multivariable logistic and ordered logistic models adjusted for age, body mass index, and diabetes were used.
